summary: Advocates a Palestinian state along the pre-1967 lines and renewed negotiations toward it.
Long-standing support for Palestinian statehood, reaffirmed by Mansour Abbas in August 2026.
Yair Golan: "My vision is two states for two peoples." Seeks a renewed push toward separation from the Palestinians.
Bennett opposes a Palestinian state and backs autonomy in Areas A and B. Lapid says he doesn't back one now but supports two states in the long term.
Eisenkot: "The two-state solution is a grave mistake." He also opposes policies that would collapse the PA or have Israel rule millions of Palestinians.
Liberman's October 2026 plan would dismantle the PA and cancel Oslo. Jordan would run civil affairs in Areas A and B while Israel keeps security control.
Both factions oppose Palestinian statehood and back strengthening settlement in Judea and Samaria.
Opposes Palestinian statehood.
Opposing a Palestinian state is a "hallmark of its security policy." Likud wants continued Israeli security control of the West Bank.
Rejects Palestinian statehood. Would disarm the PA and apply sovereignty to Areas B and C.
Both factions oppose a Palestinian state. Zehut favors "peace through victory" over territorial concessions.
Opposes Palestinian statehood and would disarm the Palestinian Authority.
UTJ has no unified territorial platform on this issue.
Opposes settlement expansion and seeks Palestinian self-determination.
Supports a Palestinian state, which rules out annexation.
Opposes annexation and pledges to dismantle illegal or newly approved outposts. Wants to curb settler violence.
Rejects a Palestinian state but opposes building in E1 because of the diplomatic cost, and criticizes settler violence. Senior candidate Yoram Cohen opposes full annexation.
Bennett wants "Israeli sovereignty over Area C" and settlement on state land. Opposes unauthorized outposts and building on private Palestinian land.
Would apply Israeli sovereignty to Area C. Jordan would administer civilian life in Areas A and B.
Backs settlement expansion in Judea and Samaria.
Supports strengthening Jewish settlement in Judea and Samaria.
Wants continued Israeli security control of the West Bank. Likud's campaign has not formally committed to annexation.
Would extend sovereignty to Areas B and C and expand settlement. Major Palestinian cities would run their own municipal affairs.
Backs Israeli sovereignty and settlement across Judea and Samaria, and has advanced the E1 project.
Pushes sovereignty and settlement expansion across Judea and Samaria.
No unified territorial platform. Its factions disagree.
Calls for "a permanent halt to fighting in Gaza" and an end to funding the war.
End Hamas rule and replace it with a Palestinian technocratic administration under international supervision, with reconstruction funded by Gulf states.
Eliminate Hamas's remaining military capabilities. Joining the government requires recognizing Hamas as a terror group "that must be destroyed." Opposes ruling millions of Palestinians.
First eliminate Hamas's military and civilian governing structures, then hand administration to an outside actor. Has floated Egyptian responsibility.
Deri has backed dismantling Hamas but also negotiated ceasefires and hostage releases.
Strike Hamas's training and arms buildup, then give it an ultimatum to disarm. Keeps Israel on the Yellow Line with freedom of military action.
Freedom of military action. Withdrawal from the Yellow Line depends on Hamas disarming. No PA rule and no Turkish or Qatari troops. Netanyahu rejected the 15-point document Hamas accepted.
Israeli control of the Gaza perimeter and the Philadelphi Corridor, plus an agency to facilitate voluntary emigration.
Continued Israeli security control and "voluntary emigration" through deals with countries willing to take Gazans.
Smotrich told Trump the plan should be canceled and wants Israeli military administration. Zehut wants to annex Gaza, remove its population, and resettle it.
Renewed Jewish settlement in Gaza and a dedicated ministry to promote emigration.
No clear Gaza policy. In July 2026 Abbas refused to say whether Hamas should be destroyed, calling the question a loyalty test.
Split: Agudat Yisrael's Goldknopf has backed resettling Gaza, while Degel HaTorah's Gafni opposes it.
Would negotiate a new nuclear agreement while keeping military measures against the program. Golan called the killing of Khamenei a strategic mistake.
The nuclear issue "must end in the destruction or dismantling of the Iranian nuclear programme." Eisenkot calls regime change unrealistic and stresses close coordination with the US.
Netanyahu calls Iran's regime an existential threat and has directed the security services to pursue its overthrow. He accepted the June 2026 halt to fighting.
Calls for regime change in Iran.
Bennett calls toppling Iran's government essential: "the clock for regime change... will start as soon as the government in Israel is changed." Lapid urged bombing energy facilities on Kharg Island.
Hadash-Ta'al MK Aida Touma-Sliman called the law discriminatory and said she opposes the death penalty in general.
Labor's Gilad Kariv called it "not moral, not Jewish and not democratic" and plans to petition the High Court.
Lapid (Yesh Atid) opposed the bill, calling it a distorted PR stunt. Bennett's own position was not reported.
Voted in favor on the instructions of its Council of Torah Sages, after the bill was amended.
Liberman voted in favor. YB has long sponsored such bills; MK Malinovsky backs the death penalty for terrorists "in principle."
Netanyahu came to vote in favor. The bill passed along coalition lines.
Sponsored the law and conditioned its budget support on it. Wants it enforced as a priority.
Would reverse the government's judicial legislation, including the changes to judicial appointments.
Pledges to preserve judicial independence while protecting the Knesset's lawmaking authority. Seeks broad agreement on a constitution.
Proposes a constitution grounded in the Declaration of Independence and broad agreement on Basic Laws and judicial review.
Wants constitutional changes that enshrine "the separation of powers."
Changes only by broad agreement: split the attorney general's role, independent judicial oversight, a Basic Law on relations between the branches.
Would split the attorney general's prosecutorial and advisory roles and create an appellate body to review High Court rulings.
Supports limiting the High Court's power to overturn legislation.
Supports limiting the High Court's power to overturn legislation.
Justice Minister Levin's reform is one of the government's flagship initiatives. Likud seeks to curb the judiciary, especially its role in appointments.
Knesset override, split AG role, ministers appoint their own legal advisers. Smotrich: "The government will be able to govern." Zehut would bar the Court from striking down laws.
Fire the AG immediately, require a two-thirds Knesset vote for Supreme Court nominees, and limit who can petition the court.
"The first decision of our government will be to establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 massacre."
"We will establish a state commission of inquiry in accordance with the law within the first five minutes."
"We support establishing a state commission of inquiry exactly according to the existing law." Members appointed by the Supreme Court president.
"Establishing a state commission of inquiry will be the first decision the party advances in the next government."
Supports a state commission under existing law, headed by a Supreme Court justice.
Supports a state commission, preferably with broad agreement on its composition.
Calls for a "comprehensive, independent and impartial investigation" but names no model. Not central to its campaign.
A special committee with state-commission powers, led by two retired judges elected by the Knesset in a secret vote, with bereaved families taking part.
Wants a "national" commission and would "under no circumstances" back a state commission. Zehut wants a neutral panel with equal coalition and opposition appointees.
No official answer. Netanyahu pushed a politically appointed "national" commission with equal coalition and opposition appointees, and opposes letting the Chief Justice appoint members.

Declined to respond to Ynet's survey.
Declined to respond to Ynet's survey.
Golan: "Only the guilty seek pardon." Netanyahu should leave public office.
Lapid: no pardon without "admission of guilt, an expression of remorse and an immediate withdrawal from political life." Bennett would back a binding deal that includes Netanyahu leaving politics.
Eisenkot: there can't be one legal system for citizens and another for Netanyahu. A pardon requires taking responsibility, admitting the offenses, and remorse.
Liberman called the request a way to "control the public discourse" and distract from the economy and the Haredi draft.
Smotrich backed the request: Netanyahu "has been persecuted for years by a corrupt judicial system."
Ben-Gvir issued a statement supporting the request.
Netanyahu filed the request without admitting guilt. Defense Minister Katz urged Herzog to grant it to heal a "deep rift."
Lapid: "It's illegal, it's corrupt, it won't pass."
Golan said the government had abandoned reason.
Liberman said the move aims to distract from the hostage crisis, the draft-dodging law, and the refusal to set up a state inquiry.
Shas ministers sat in the cabinet that unanimously voted no confidence in the AG in March 2025.
The Likud-led cabinet unanimously voted to remove the AG, led by Justice Minister Levin.
Its ministers voted with the unanimous cabinet to oust the AG. Wants the AG's advisory and prosecutorial roles split.
Its platform demands the attorney general be dismissed immediately.
Netanyahu called the 2021 term-limit bill "Iranian-style," arguing it takes the choice away from voters. (Most recent explicit statement found.)
Would limit prime ministers to two terms and cap the number of ministers.
Eight-year limit on the premiership, starting with Bennett.
Proposes limiting prime ministers to two terms and cutting the number of ministers.
Eight-year / two-term limit for prime ministers.
Wants a law shielding yeshiva students from compulsory service and won't join a government that doesn't pass one.
Won't join a government without a law preserving sweeping exemptions. Somewhat more open than UTJ to recruitment targets.
Favors encouraging Haredi enlistment through incentives rather than coercion.
Smotrich backs exemptions for full-time yeshiva students but wants other Haredi men to enlist. Zehut wants a month of basic training for all men.
Netanyahu: "Whoever does not study Torah will enlist." Opened the door to sanctions, but still supports exemptions for full-time students.
A Basic Law on service obligations, with at most 25% of each Haredi cohort recognized as Torah students. Winter won't join a government until it passes.
Compulsory service for all. Torah deferrals capped at 3% of a cohort, and evaders face criminal penalties and loss of benefits.
Mandatory service for all. Bennett: "I will not put them in prison, but they will not receive a shekel from the state."
Universal military or civilian service, with the IDF choosing recruits first and benefits withdrawn from evaders.
Universal military or civilian service. Evaders would lose benefits and public-sector jobs and face travel and voting restrictions.
Service for all from age 18. Hendel: "Anyone who chooses not to serve... gets nothing from the state." Proposes stripping voting rights from evaders.
Rejects a state-imposed national-service arrangement. Any framework must be agreed with the Arab community's leadership.
Proposed a civilian-service framework for young Arab citizens, focused on jobs and community work rather than compulsory enlistment.
"Universal military or civilian service."
Mandatory service for all.
Compulsory military or civilian service for all population groups, explicitly including Haredim and Arabs.
Universal military or civilian service that applies to Haredim and Arabs, with sanctions for evaders.
Military or civilian service from age 18 for all Israelis, including Haredi and Arab citizens.
Prioritizes childcare subsidies, family assistance, and funding for Haredi institutions.
Seeks continued state support for yeshivas and welfare for Haredi families.
Has opened the door to legal consequences for draft dodgers while keeping exemptions for full-time students.
Evaders without an exemption lose benefits and face criminal penalties.
Withdraw benefits from draft evaders.
Evaders "will not receive a shekel." Would withdraw yeshiva stipends, municipal-tax discounts, and childcare subsidies.
Evaders lose state benefits and are barred from public-sector jobs.
"Anyone who chooses not to serve in the State of Israel gets nothing from the state."
Civil marriage and divorce, recognition of non-Orthodox conversions.
Would introduce "civil marriage and divorce." Strongly secular, favoring separation of religion and state.
Lapid: "there should be a parallel civil marriage option for anyone who wants it." Proposes civil-union registration with marriage-equivalent rights.
Seeks a greater role for Jewish law and values in public life and stresses the state's Jewish character.
Keep Orthodox authority over marriage, conversion, and religious services. Opposes civil marriage.
Keep Orthodox authority over marriage, conversion, and religious services. Opposes civil marriage.
The platform stresses Israel's "Jewish-democratic character" but takes no explicit position on civil marriage.
"Public transportation on Shabbat, with local discretion over services."
Allowed according to local circumstances. Municipalities would control business opening hours.
Shabbat public transport decided locally.
Resists expanding public transportation on Shabbat.
Resists expanding public transportation on Shabbat and wants the religious status quo preserved.
"An end to the Chief Rabbinate's monopoly over kosher certification."
Restore competition in kosher certification.
Recognize international kosher certification to lower food prices.
Zelekha: open kosher certification to competing rabbis under government supervision.
Keep Orthodox authority over religious services.
Keep Orthodox authority over religious services.
Seeks public funding for Haredi schools while protecting their autonomy, even where the full core curriculum isn't taught.
Seeks public funding for Haredi schools while protecting their autonomy, even where the full core curriculum isn't taught.
Zehut: parental control, school vouchers, and lighter core requirements, but no vouchers for schools that drop core studies entirely.
Core studies alongside Jewish and Zionist values.
"Compulsory core studies" in math, English, and Hebrew, plus stronger Jewish education.
All schools must teach the full core curriculum, including math and English.
End special funding for Haredi school networks that don't teach core subjects.

Netanyahu says the status quo "would not change" and that Ben-Gvir's moves are coordinated with him. He told the cabinet that Jewish prayer "does not breach" the status quo. Some Likud ministers warned Ben-Gvir is "reckless."
Backs expanding Jewish prayer. Smotrich has called for a synagogue on the Mount, and Zehut would remove the Islamic Waqf.
Promotes Jewish prayer on the Mount as a religious necessity and an expression of sovereignty.
"Equal marriage, adoption and surrogacy rights for same-sex couples."
Lapid: legislation within 100 days "that says the rights of every couple in Israel will be equal." Bennett, who once opposed it, says his government would "advance same-sex marriage."
A UTJ lawmaker called the LGBTQ community "the most dangerous thing for the State of Israel" (2023). Haredi lawmakers seek to roll back rights.
Nationalize privatized companies, cap rent at 20%, create a state mortgage bank, free education, a 30% capital-gains tax.
A larger state role: shorter work week, expanded childcare and public housing, stronger unions, action against monopolies.
Focuses on low-income households and food assistance. Deri tied budget support to food-voucher funding.
Housing for Haredi communities, childcare subsidies, family assistance.
Cut regulation, open imports, break up monopolies. Also subsidized housing and higher benefits for low-pension seniors.
Competition plus public investment: remove import barriers, curb monopolies, invest in infrastructure in the north and south.
Market competition: European standards, lower agricultural tariffs, a target of "cutting supermarket-basket prices by 30% within three years."
Generally free-market, cutting regulation ("What's Good for Europe is Good for Israel"), though some MKs back interventionist measures.
Break up monopolies, remove import barriers, reduce bureaucracy, plus urban renewal in the periphery.
RZP leans free-market but uses intervention such as childcare subsidies and bank taxes. Zehut wants a flat income tax and land privatization.
New Economic Party: cut VAT from 18% to 12% over six years, abolish food tariffs and quotas, lower income and corporate taxes.
Balad seeks to replace the Jewish-national constitutional framework with a "state of all its citizens" and end official recognition of Zionist institutions.
Abbas: "The Jewish character of the state is a reality imposed upon us." Arab parties accept it in practice and focus on equality.
Proposes a constitution grounded in the 1948 Declaration of Independence.
Joining the government requires accepting Israel's "Jewish-democratic character" and upholding the Declaration of Independence.
Seeks a greater role for Jewish law and values in public life.

Member of the "Change bloc," whose priority is a government without Netanyahu.

Change bloc. Liberman calls Netanyahu Deri's "puppet."
Won't join a coalition but may give outside support to a non-Netanyahu government. "There is no automatic support."
Has sought a role in an Eisenkot-led government.
Will recommend "whoever brings the most Zionist seats." Open to a Netanyahu–Eisenkot–Bennett unity government.
In the Netanyahu bloc, but divided: Asher is open to serving under Eisenkot, while Porush rejects that.
Stays with Netanyahu. Deri favors a broad Netanyahu-led government that includes Eisenkot.
Backs Netanyahu for PM while trying to change the right's direction from within.
Netanyahu bloc, with a surplus-vote deal with Likud.
Netanyahu bloc. Opposes a broad coalition with Yashar or Together.
Netanyahu's own party.
Seeks to enter government, and is the most open of the Arab parties to joining one.
Golan: "Yes, with Ra'am. Jewish-Arab partnership in government is a positive thing."
Won't join a coalition on principle, but offers conditional outside support for a minority government.
Ruled out Ra'am under its current positions, but left a minority government relying on Arab votes open.
Bennett "ruled out another coalition with Ra'am," whether as a partner or as outside support for a minority government.
Rules out "a coalition containing haredi or Arab parties" and any minority government relying on them.
Won't give decisive votes to any government that depends on Arab or Haredi parties.
Kahanist and hardline on Israeli Arabs.
A Haredi party. Will join only a government that passes an exemption law.
A Haredi party. Will join only a government that passes an exemption law.
Its likely partners include Shas and United Torah Judaism.
Its likely partners include Shas and UTJ.

Sources differ: JNS says Bennett hasn't explicitly excluded Haredi parties, while the Jerusalem Post reports he rules out coalition deals with them. He insists on universal service either way.
Wants a government whose majority does not depend on the Haredi parties.
Rules out a coalition containing Haredi parties.
Won't give decisive votes to a government that depends on Haredi parties.
